name: Kichwa
variant: Kichwa of Ecuador (Northern Quechua), unified spelling
region: The highlands and Amazon of Ecuador: Imbabura, Pichincha, Cotopaxi, Tungurahua, Chimborazo, Bolívar, Cañar, Azuay, Loja, Napo, Pastaza, Orellana and Sucumbíos
summary: The most widely spoken Indigenous language of Ecuador, from the páramos of the Andes to the rivers of the Amazon. An official language of intercultural relations since 2008.

conjugator.label: Verb
conjugator.hint: Type the verb as in the dictionary, ending in -na: mikuna «eat», rimana «speak», rina «go», munana «want». You can also type just the root (miku).

own.hint: Type any verb ending in -na and its meaning in English. The endings are the same for every verb.

source.short: Múgica, Aprendamos kichwa; Kichwa Yachakukkunapak Shimiyuk Kamu (2009)
source.full: Mons. Alejandro Múgica, Aprendamos kichwa: gramática kichwa actualizada (Napo), for the verb; Aprenda usted mismo el quichua, for the highland forms; Ministerio de Educación del Ecuador, Kichwa Yachakukkunapak Shimiyuk Kamu (Quito, 2009), for the unified spelling and the vocabulary. As a historical reference: Juan M. Grimm, La lengua quichua (dialecto de la República del Ecuador) (Freiburg: Herder, 1896). Unified spelling (shukyachishka killkay).

about: Kichwa is the Ecuadorian form of Quechua, the family of languages that stretches along the Andes from Colombia to Argentina. It is spoken by hundreds of thousands of people of peoples such as the Otavalo, Kayambi, Panzaleo, Salasaka, Puruhá, Kañari and Saraguro in the highlands, and by the Amazonian Kichwa of Napo, Pastaza, Orellana and Sucumbíos.

It split from southern Quechua centuries ago: it has only three written vowels, a single «we» (ñukanchik), and it lost the personal possessive suffixes. Each province has its own pronunciation, so since 1980 it has been written in a unified spelling that everyone reads the same way.

The 2008 Constitution recognises it, together with Shuar, as an official language of intercultural relations. It is taught in intercultural bilingual schools and kept alive by radio stations, musicians, writers and the Kichwa Language Academy.

orthography.intro: We use the unified Kichwa spelling (shukyachishka killkay), the one of the Ministry of Education and of the Kichwa Yachakukkunapak Shimiyuk Kamu dictionary (2009). Each sound has one letter: k for /k/ before any vowel, w and y for the glides, and only three vowels.
notes: There are only three vowels. Next to an old q, an r or an ll, i and u sometimes sound like e and o (urku «hill» sounds «orco»), but they are always written i and u.
k is written before any vowel: killa «moon», kuyana «love». The c, qu, g, e, o and hu of the old spelling (quichua, huasi, Cayambe) are not used.
After n, m and other consonants k often sounds like g and t like d: -nki is said «-ngi», -nchik «-nchij», tanta «tanda». It is written the same everywhere.

h is a soft breath (hatun «big»), and the final -k of -nchik or mikuk often sounds like a Spanish j or drops. ll is said like the «lli» of «million» in Imbabura and like a «zh» in the central highlands.
Stress falls on the second-to-last syllable and isn't written: mikuni, rimarkanki.
The unified alphabet also has z and zh, which, like ts, are found in a few words of some provinces. Older texts, such as Grimm's grammar (1896), use c, qu, hu and e, o: «huasi», «micuna».

grammar.intro: A Kichwa verb is a root and a chain of suffixes: first those that change the meaning (-chi, -ri, -pa, -naku), then the tense, and last the person. The root is the infinitive without -na: mikuna → miku-.

items.description: -chi make someone do, -ri for oneself, -naku each other, -pa for someone, -mu towards here…

blocks.title: The persons
blocks.description: There is a single «we», ñukanchik. The past adds -rka-, and the future has endings of its own in the 1st and 3rd persons.

blocks.title: Verb forms without person
blocks.description: These forms carry no person and link clauses together.

cells: when someone else eats, if someone else eats

blocks.title: Suffixes that change the verb
blocks.description: They go between the root and the tense, and they can be combined.

blocks.title: Who to whom
blocks.description: With -wa- the action goes towards me. Towards other people the pronoun is used with -ta.

tenses.name: Present
tenses.description: Kunan pacha: what happens now or always.

tenses.name: -shka past
tenses.description: What has happened, or turned out to have happened (-shka-).

tenses.name: Past habitual
tenses.description: What one used to do: -k and karkani.

tenses.name: Imperative
tenses.description: Orders to you or you all (-y, -ychik).

tenses.name: Let's
tenses.description: Inviting others to do something together (-shun), like the ñukanchik future.
